summary: Describes unknown key-share attacks against the use of DTLS-SRTP, and against the identity bindings used in WebRTC and SIP identity. In such attacks one party can be tricked about who it is really sharing keys with. The document explains the attacks and suggests mitigations. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Imagine you whisper a secret code to a friend, but a trickster makes your friend believe the code came from someone else. This document explains such mix-ups in secure calls and how to stop them.

questions: what is an unknown key share attack
how to protect dtls-srtp from identity attacks
how to prevent identity misbinding in webrtc
subtitle: How an attacker can make a caller think they reached the wrong person over DTLS-SRTP, and the two TLS extensions that stop it.

tldr.problem: In DTLS-SRTP, peers authenticate each other by matching a certificate fingerprint from the SDP signaling. An attacker can copy someone else's fingerprint, or bind their own identity to it, so that a victim is misled about who is on the other end of the call.
tldr.mechanism: Two TLS extensions carry signaling data inside the handshake, where the Finished message protects it. The external_id_hash extension carries a SHA-256 hash of the identity assertion, and the external_session_id extension carries the SDP tls-id value.
tldr.outcome: With the extensions, a peer that sees mismatched values aborts the handshake. RFC 8122 is updated to recommend them. They defend against the identity-binding attack, and against the fingerprint attack when signaling integrity holds.

today: RFC 8844 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 8122 to recommend its mitigations.

sections.title: Why Fingerprints Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Secure calls that use SDP (the Session Description Protocol) with DTLS-SRTP do their key agreement with TLS or DTLS. Authentication is tied back to the signaling by certificate fingerprints: a peer checks that a hash in the SDP matches the certificate used in the handshake.

WebRTC identity and SIP identity add a binding between an external identity and those fingerprints. That binding is not integrity protected, so it is open to an identity misbinding attack, also called an unknown key-share (UKS) attack. The attacker binds their own identity to the fingerprint of another entity, and peers end up confused about who they are talking to.

This document updates RFC 8122 to recommend two mitigations. It assumes that signaling is integrity protected, though it notes that many SDP deployments do not guarantee that.
sections.eli5: A fingerprint is like a name tag for a computer. The trouble is that a trickster can stick someone else's name tag on and fool people about who is who.

sections.title: The Unknown Key-Share Attack
sections.content:
In a UKS attack, a malicious participant claims to control a key that really belongs to someone else. It happens when the identity tied to a key is not properly bound to that key. An endpoint that gets another entity's fingerprint can advertise it as its own in SDP.

The attack does not give the attacker access to confidential information exchanged between the victims. The harm is the failed mutual authentication: a victim might send information to the wrong entity, or misread information whose context was misrepresented.

Two limits apply when signaling integrity holds. An attacker can only change the parts of signaling they produce themselves (their own offers and answers), and nobody sets up a session with a peer they are unwilling to talk to. So attacks must join two separate sessions into one. Systems with strong identity bindings assume a stronger attacker who can both watch and modify signaling.

Key continuity, as in ZRTP or as recommended in RFC 8122, might reveal the attack if the user had a session with the attacker or the real peer before. Whether it does depends on how the implementation stores identities and keys.
sections.eli5: The trickster cannot read your messages, but they can make you think you are writing to the wrong person. You might say something to the wrong kid, or the right kid might misunderstand it.

sections.title: Attack on Identity Bindings and the external_id_hash Extension
sections.content:
WebRTC identity assertions and the PASSporT token used in SIP identity are bound to an endpoint's certificate fingerprint. The authority certifying the binding does not have to check that the requester controls the keys behind the fingerprint. In the example, the attacker Mallory gets a binding of her identity to Patsy's fingerprint (P) and shows it to Norma. A correct binding for Norma is shown to Patsy. A DTLS session then forms directly between Norma and Patsy. Patsy rightly believes she is talking to Norma, but Norma believes she is talking to Mallory.

The fix follows the SIGMA idea: put the identity under a MAC in the handshake. In TLS the Finished message covers the whole handshake, so a TLS extension is enough. The external_id_hash extension carries a SHA-256 hash of the identity assertion, in an ExternalIdentityHash struct with a binding_hash field of 0 to 32 bytes. An empty value shows support, or that the sender has no binding.

  • A peer receiving a value that does not match its peer's binding MUST fail the handshake with an illegal_parameter alert. A zero-length extension is required if the peer gave no binding.
  • A binding_hash of any length other than 0 or 32 MUST cause a fatal decode_error alert.
  • A peer that gets a binding but no extension MAY accept the connection, since older implementations will lack it for some time.
  • In TLS 1.3 a server sends the extension in EncryptedExtensions.

For WebRTC identity, the hash is SHA-256(b64decode(identity-assertion-value)), taken over the raw decoded octets with no canonicalization. For PASSporT, the compact form MUST be expanded to the full form, and the hash is SHA-256(b64decode(signed-identity-digest)).
sections.eli5: The fix is to seal the name tag inside the secret handshake. If the name tag someone shows you does not match the one sealed in the handshake, you stop right away.

sections.title: Attack on Fingerprints and the external_session_id Extension
sections.content:
Even with trustworthy signaling, an attacker can confuse peers if one endpoint reuses a certificate across calls. In the example, Norma starts two sessions at almost the same time: one with Mallory, who falsely uses Patsy's fingerprint, and one with Patsy. Mallory forwards DTLS and media between Norma and Patsy, and lets Patsy's session complete so Patsy believes it worked. The RFC itself calls the needed conditions somewhat implausible: Norma must run two sessions nearly at once with the same certificate, and Mallory must be on the media path. Where ICE is used, Mallory must also make sure connectivity checks succeed.

The fix gives each session a unique identifier. The SDP tls-id attribute is already required to be unique, so the new external_session_id extension carries it in the handshake, where the Finished message protects it. The struct is ExternalSessionId, with a session_id of 20 to 255 bytes, holding the tls-id value in ASCII.

  • The extension goes in the ClientHello, and in the ServerHello (TLS and DTLS before 1.3) or EncryptedExtensions (TLS 1.3) if the client sent it.
  • Endpoints MUST check that the value matches the tls-id they received in their peer's session description, and otherwise abort with a fatal illegal_parameter alert.
  • An endpoint MAY continue without the extension to interoperate with peers that lack it.

This defense fails if an attacker can rewrite tls-id values in signaling. Only external_id_hash can resist an attacker who compromises signaling integrity.
sections.eli5: Give each phone call its own secret ticket number and check it inside the handshake. If the ticket number does not match, the call is stopped.

sections.title: Third-Party Call Control and Session Concatenation
sections.content:
Third-party call control (3PCC, described in RFC 3725) lets a signaling peer set up a call that a different entity ends. A UKS attack looks much like some 3PCC practices. The mitigations here will block 3PCC if peers disagree on identities or on tls-id values. A controller that follows RFC 3725 and forwards SDP unmodified, or at least leaves the fingerprint, tls-id and identity attributes alone, keeps working.

Session concatenation is a limit of the session-identifier defense. An attacker who sets up two concurrent sessions with different peers and forwards signaling between them can make the peers connect directly while each thinks it is talking to the attacker. Peer authentication such as WebRTC identity or SIP identity prevents that single-connection form.

Because several connections can exist in one signaling session, the RFC adds two MUST NOT rules. Information from a TLS connection MUST NOT be used in a secondary protocol that assumes the signaling peer is the same. Security-sensitive information from one TLS connection MUST NOT be used in other TLS connections of the same session.
sections.eli5: If a grown-up arranges a call for two other people, the new checks might think it is a trick. And a trickster can still pass notes between two calls, so what you learn on one call should not be trusted on another.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
With identity assertions, the mitigations ensure that TLS peers cannot be misrepresented, even if an attacker modifies signaling. Without identity assertions, they prevent the session splicing attack on fingerprints. Defending against session concatenation also requires that protocol peers cannot claim other entities' certificate fingerprints.

IANA registered two extensions in the TLS ExtensionType Values registry: external_id_hash with code point 55 and external_session_id with code point 56. Both are recommended and marked "CH, EE" in TLS 1.3.

If SHA-256 proves inadequate, the RFC says a new extension that uses a different hash function can be defined.
sections.eli5: The checks stop the name-tag trick when the details are sealed in. The only extra thing needed to stop the note-passing trick is making sure nobody can copy another person's name tag.
